summary: For ages 5–8, teach evidence-based comparison of two engineering designs that solve the same problem: test both the SAME way, record each one's performance, then recommend the better-performing design by citing the recorded data (not preference or looks), name a strength AND weakness of each, and suggest one improvement. The central move beyond a single test is that the recommendation must rest on what the numbers/observations showed. The same test–record–compare loop works with other same-problem contexts (two bridge shapes, two boat hulls, two shade structures). The strongest version has children generate the head-to-head data through their own fair tests; pre-authored scenes, dialogue, and scored questions can support interpretation and vocabulary but do not let the child produce the comparison themselves.
misconceptions: Recommending the design you liked or built rather than the one the data supports.
Testing the two designs differently, making the comparison unfair.
Seeing only a 'winner' and missing that each design has strengths and weaknesses.
Judging on appearance rather than measured performance.
Not recording results, so the comparison rests on memory or feeling.
Thinking the better design needs no improvement.

activities.title: Best Design Wins: testing two bridges with a shared load
steps: Set up two designs for the same problem — e.g. a flat bridge and an arched bridge made from the same material and spanning the same gap (or, as alternatives, two boat hulls floated the same way, or two shade structures compared by how much light gets through — judged by the cast shadow or transmitted light patch on the ground — and/or by how cool the shaded spot stays, checked with a thermometer or hand touch over the same time; never by looking toward the sun or holding material up to the eyes).
State out loud what you will keep the same for both (same gap, same way of adding weight, same exposure time) before you start, so the test is fair.
Add weights (toy bricks or marbles) to the first design one at a time, and record the number it held before it sagged or dropped (e.g. flat bridge held 8).
Test the second design exactly the same way and record its number (e.g. arch held 12).
Fill both numbers into a side-by-side comparison chart (Design A row vs Design B row).
Recommend which design performed better and point to the recorded numbers as your reason.
Say one way you would improve the weaker design, linked to why it underperformed.
activities.insight: The recorded data — not your favourite or the one you built — shows which design performed better on the measure you tested, and you can point to the numbers to prove it.

activities.title: Trade-offs: when each design wins on a different measure
steps: Choose a problem where each design can win on a different measure — e.g. one bridge holds more weight but the other is quicker to build or uses less paper.
Test and record each design on BOTH measures (e.g. weight held, and time or material used).
Tag each design with a strength and a weakness based on the records.
Explain why there is no single 'best' — each design has trade-offs — and recommend one for a stated purpose, citing which measure mattered most.
activities.insight: Real designs have trade-offs: one design can be strong on one measure and weak on another, so the recommendation depends on which measure matters for the problem.

activities.title: Read the results chart and defend the pick (interpretation practice)
steps: Look at a small side-by-side results table for two designs tested on the same problem.
Decide which design the data supports as better for the stated problem.
Reject a 'liked it more' or 'looks stronger' reason and give the data-based reason instead.
Match each design to its strength and its weakness from the table; sort listed features into strengths vs weaknesses.
activities.insight: An evidence-based recommendation reads the recorded results and names strengths and weaknesses, rather than relying on appearance or preference.

activities.title: Justify-it dialogue: pressing for evidence and a weakness
steps: After running the two tests, answer a prompt like 'the data shows A held more — so which do you recommend, and what's a weakness of A?'
Point to the specific result that supports the recommendation.
Name a weakness of the design you chose, not just its strength.
Answer a follow-up on how you'd check your improvement actually helped.
activities.insight: A good recommendation can be defended by pointing to evidence and still acknowledges the chosen design's weaknesses.

checkQuestion: Here are two paper bridges that were built to solve the same problem: hold as many marbles as possible across this gap. Test both, keep a record of how each one does, and then tell me which design is better and why — and one thing you'd change to improve it. (Provide the two bridges, marbles, and a way to record; watch how the child tests and what they base the verdict on.)
checkAnswer: The child tests both bridges under the same conditions, records each one's performance (e.g. marbles held before collapse), compares the recorded results to name each design's strength and weakness, and recommends the better design by pointing to the data — then suggests an improvement tied to why the weaker one failed.
